quotes.text: You probably think this is a licensing problem, but the real tension is that copilot is only as good as the data underneath it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: Copilot removes the blank page problem and the syntax problem, and it doesn't remove the thinking problem because you still have to know what question you're asking
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: If the thing you want has a conversation in it, you probably want an agent. If it just runs on a schedule and nobody talks to it, you want a flow.

quotes.text: The boring work of naming things well and describing them is what makes the AI worth having, and no feature update replaces that work.

quotes.text: The honest judgment is that Copilot Studio is good, and the failure mode is using it for everything because you already paid for it.

takeaways: Copilot in Power Platform is four surfaces, not one: Power Apps, Power Automate and Power BI help you build, while Copilot Studio builds agents that answer on their own.
Answer quality is capped by your data and instructions, so prepare semantic models and name Dataverse tables and columns clearly before relying on Copilot.
Agent cost is a design decision: credits vary by answer type, internal agents for Microsoft 365 Copilot seat holders consume no credits, and exceeding prepaid capacity can disable agents.
hook: Copilot was supposed to clear busy work, yet in Power Platform it often feels like one more thing to check. This episode explains the four Copilot surfaces for makers, analysts and admins, what Copilot Studio agents really cost, and where they work or fall apart. You'll learn how to prepare your data and design agents so the bill and the answers stay under control.
